title: Lec 06 — Aortic Valve Disease
subtitle: Week 01 · Lec 06 · Aortic Valve Disease | 20 questions

questions.text: A 67-year-old woman with a bicuspid aortic valve is found to have severe aortic stenosis. Left heart catheterization records LV systolic pressure of 210 mmHg against an aortic systolic pressure of 120 mmHg. Which statement best describes the primary pathophysiologic consequence of this obstruction?
options: The stenotic valve allows diastolic regurgitation into the LV, raising preload and initiating eccentric hypertrophy as the primary derangement
The narrowed orifice traps blood in the left atrium, elevating pulmonary venous pressure as the primary hemodynamic consequence
The stenotic valve creates resistance to forward ejection, imposing pressure overload that increases LV afterload
The transvalvular gradient reduces subendocardial perfusion time, making ischemia the sole primary driver of LV dysfunction
questions.explanation:
Aortic stenosis creates resistance to forward flow, and this increased afterload is the primary pathophysiologic mechanism from which all downstream consequences — LVH, diastolic dysfunction, ischemia, and eventual systolic dysfunction — derive. The lecture states verbatim: "stenosis provides resistance to forward flow or an increased afterload" and that "remodeling and hemodynamic effects are all a result of increased afterload." The 90 mmHg transvalvular gradient in this patient reflects the excess pressure the LV must generate above aortic pressure to eject blood through the stenotic orifice.
Option A is incorrect: regurgitant flow across the valve is a feature of aortic regurgitation, not stenosis; AS impedes forward flow rather than permitting backward flow into the LV.
Option B is incorrect: the primary hemodynamic insult of AS falls on the left ventricle; elevated left atrial pressure is a downstream consequence of impaired LV compliance, not the primary mechanism.
Option D is incorrect: while ischemia results from the supply-demand mismatch of LVH, it is a downstream consequence of increased afterload and the resulting hypertrophic remodeling, not the primary pathophysiologic event.

questions.text: A 74-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis undergoes echocardiography confirming significant concentric LV hypertrophy. His cardiologist explains that while LVH is initially compensatory, it carries two major harmful consequences. Which pair correctly identifies these harms?
options: Stiff LV impairing diastolic filling with elevated filling pressures, and myocardial ischemia from supply-demand mismatch
Hyperdynamic ejection with accelerated ventricular emptying, and paradoxical splitting of S2 from delayed aortic valve closure
Elevated right ventricular preload from ventricular interdependence, and functional tricuspid regurgitation from annular dilation
Atrial dilation from elevated LA pressure causing left atrial thrombosis, and paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale
questions.explanation:
The two cardinal harms of LVH in aortic stenosis are impaired diastolic function — the stiff LV raises filling pressures and promotes pulmonary congestion — and myocardial ischemia from supply-demand mismatch. The lecture explicitly calls these "the bad," naming impaired diastolic function leading to increased filling pressure and pulmonary congestion, and myocardial ischemia due to supply-demand mismatch. Eventual myocardial fibrosis and systolic dysfunction are the end-stage sequelae of these ongoing insults.
Option B is incorrect: LVH in AS typically reduces, not accelerates, ejection kinetics as the stiff ventricle compensates for pressure overload; hyperdynamic ejection describes a volume-overload state.
Option C is incorrect: right ventricular consequences are not among the primary taught harms of AS-related LVH; the lecture focuses on left-sided diastolic dysfunction and ischemia.
Option D is incorrect: while elevated LA pressure is a downstream consequence of diastolic dysfunction, left atrial thrombosis and paradoxical embolism are not among the named LVH harms listed in this lecture.
Slide 16 · Transcript 0:12:00

questions.text: A 69-year-old man with severe calcific aortic stenosis presents after losing consciousness while climbing a flight of stairs. He had no prodrome and recovered spontaneously within 30 seconds. Resting BP is 118/74 mmHg and HR is 82/min. What is the physiologic basis for exertional syncope in aortic stenosis?
options: Increased LV filling pressures during exertion trigger reflex inhibition of the SA node via atrial baroreceptors, producing transient sinus arrest with loss of cardiac output
Exertional tachycardia shortens diastolic filling time, acutely reducing LV stroke volume to the point of triggering ventricular fibrillation and loss of consciousness
Vagal activation during peak exertion causes transient complete AV block, dropping cardiac output below the cerebral autoregulation threshold of perfusion pressure
Systemic vasodilation occurs normally with exercise, but the fixed stenosis prevents any rise in cardiac output, leaving cerebral perfusion reduced
questions.explanation:
Exertional syncope in aortic stenosis occurs because the normal vasodilatory response to exercise is not compensated by an increase in cardiac output — the stenotic valve limits stroke volume augmentation, and cerebral perfusion falls. The lecture states directly: "exertional syncope is because of reduced cerebral perfusion...your systemic vasculature dilates, your SVR decreases, and your cardiac output increases" — but in AS the cardiac output cannot increase through the fixed orifice. This hemodynamic mechanism is distinct from arrhythmic syncope.
Option A is incorrect: atrial baroreceptor-mediated SA node inhibition is not the described syncope mechanism in AS; the lecture identifies a hemodynamic fixed-output cause, not a neural reflex arrhythmia.
Option B is incorrect: ventricular fibrillation is an arrhythmic mechanism inconsistent with the brief, spontaneous recovery described; exertional syncope in AS is hemodynamic.
Option C is incorrect: complete AV block is not the mechanism the lecture identifies; vagal AV block is a separate entity from the fixed-output hemodynamic explanation offered here.
Slide 21 · Transcript 0:17:27

questions.text: Two patients are referred for aortic stenosis workup. Patient A is a 58-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve identified in childhood, now reporting exertional dyspnea. Patient B is an 82-year-old woman with no prior valve history presenting with angina and near-syncope. Which statement best reflects the expected age-related symptom onset pattern for each patient's type of aortic stenosis?
options: Patient A's bicuspid valve is expected to remain asymptomatic into his 80s, presenting later than the calcific disease in Patient B
Patient A's bicuspid valve causes symptoms typically in the 50s–70s; Patient B's calcific stenosis typically becomes symptomatic after age 70
Both patients have the same timeline because symptom onset is determined solely by gradient severity, not by the underlying valve anatomy
Patient B's calcific stenosis is an aggressive form that typically presents before age 70, while bicuspid stenosis typically presents after age 80
questions.explanation:
Bicuspid aortic valve disease produces stenosis that becomes symptomatic at a younger age — typically 50–70 years — compared with calcific degenerative stenosis, which usually presents after age 70. The lecture states: "Symptoms usually begin age 50-70 in bicuspid valves, age >70 in calcific stenosis," noting that bicuspid patients present "more in middle age, like 50s, 60s, 70s" while calcific disease presents in the "70s or 80s." Patient A's presentation at age 58 fits the bicuspid timeline; Patient B at 82 fits the calcific timeline.
Option A is incorrect: bicuspid AS presents earlier, not later, than calcific AS; this answer reverses the two timelines.
Option C is incorrect: valve anatomy does alter the onset timeline — bicuspid valves develop fibrosis and calcification decades earlier than trileaflet valves because of abnormal leaflet stress patterns.
Option D is incorrect: calcific AS is a slowly progressive disease of older age; the lecture places its symptom onset after age 70, not before; bicuspid disease presents earlier, not later.
Slide 21 · Transcript 0:18:27

questions.text: A medical student presents a patient with severe aortic stenosis confirmed by echocardiography (valve area 0.7 cm², mean gradient 55 mmHg). She notes the systolic murmur is soft, grade 2/6, and argues this makes the echocardiographic diagnosis questionable. How should you address her reasoning?
options: Murmur intensity is not a reliable indicator of stenosis severity — in low-output states, severe AS can produce a soft murmur despite critical obstruction
The echocardiographic criteria should be repeated because a valve area below 1.0 cm² reliably generates at least a grade 4/6 murmur in a patient with adequate cardiac output
A soft murmur reliably indicates a gradient below 40 mmHg and stenosis of at most moderate severity, regardless of echocardiographic findings
Murmur intensity correlates directly with severity in AS and should be used as the primary bedside method for grading stenosis in clinical practice
questions.explanation:
Murmur intensity is not a reliable indicator of severity, per the lecture: intensity does not equate to stenosis severity in aortic stenosis. The lecture states this explicitly — "The intensity is not always equal to the severity" — and repeats the point in the key-point summary slide. In low-output states (which can occur in severe AS with reduced stroke volume or reduced LV function), the turbulent flow velocity across the valve diminishes, softening the murmur even when the anatomic obstruction is critical. Echocardiographic Doppler criteria (valve area, jet velocity, mean gradient) are the standard for severity assessment.
Option B is incorrect: the lecture directly contradicts this; a grade 4/6 cutoff for severe AS is not a physiologic or clinical rule, and low-output states can produce soft murmurs despite severe disease.
Option C is incorrect: a soft murmur does not exclude severe AS; hemodynamic severity and acoustic intensity are dissociated in low-flow states.
Option D is incorrect: the lecture explicitly teaches the opposite principle; bedside murmur intensity is an unreliable proxy for aortic stenosis severity.
Slide 22 · Transcript 0:19:33

questions.text: On physical examination of a patient with aortic stenosis, the harsh systolic murmur peaks very late in systole, and palpation of the right carotid reveals a pulse that is weak in amplitude and slow to rise compared to the cardiac apex beat. What do these combined findings indicate?
options: An early-peaking murmur with a weak carotid pulse indicates mild AS with concurrent right-sided heart failure reducing right-sided output

The late-peaking murmur is a non-specific finding; a weak carotid pulse alone reflects reduced output from any cause and cannot reliably localize the problem to the aortic valve without additional clinical context
A late-peaking murmur with a bounding, full carotid pulse is the classic profile of severe AS with preserved cardiac output
A later-peaking systolic murmur indicates greater AS severity; the weak and delayed carotid upstroke — parvus (small) and tardus (slow) — reflects impaired ejection across the stenotic valve
questions.explanation:
In aortic stenosis, a later-peaking systolic murmur indicates greater stenosis severity, and the blunted, delayed carotid upstroke (parvus et tardus) reflects the reduced rate and volume of blood ejected across the narrowed orifice. The lecture states: "we describe the murmur as late peaking, being more severe," and describes the classic pulse finding as "a blunted carotid upstroke, it's gonna be weak and late." Together, late murmur peaking and parvus et tardus consistently point to hemodynamically significant obstruction.
Option A is incorrect: an early-peaking murmur suggests milder AS; the weak carotid pulse in this context arises from left-sided obstruction, not right heart failure.
Option B is incorrect: while a weak pulse can occur in low-output states of any cause, the combination of a late-peaking systolic murmur at the base radiating to the carotids specifically points to AS.
Option C is incorrect: bounding pulses with wide pulse pressure are the hallmark of aortic regurgitation, not stenosis; a late-peaking murmur with bounding pulses would be a contradictory combination in AS.
Slide 22 · Transcript 0:19:14

questions.text: A 73-year-old woman with known aortic stenosis undergoes echocardiography with Doppler interrogation. You review the transaortic flow data. Which combination of findings meets the echocardiographic threshold for severe aortic stenosis?
options: Peak transaortic jet velocity 3.4 m/s, mean gradient 31 mmHg, aortic valve area 1.4 cm²
Peak transaortic jet velocity 3.8 m/s, mean gradient 37 mmHg, aortic valve area 1.2 cm²
Peak transaortic jet velocity 4.6 m/s, mean gradient 48 mmHg, aortic valve area 0.8 cm²
Peak transaortic jet velocity 4.2 m/s, mean gradient 42 mmHg, aortic valve area 1.1 cm²
questions.explanation:
The echocardiographic criteria for severe aortic stenosis are peak transaortic jet velocity greater than 4 m/s, mean gradient greater than 40 mmHg, and aortic valve area less than 1.0 cm². Only option C satisfies all three thresholds: velocity 4.6 m/s (>4), mean gradient 48 mmHg (>40), and valve area 0.8 cm² (<1.0). The lecture teaches that Doppler interrogation assessing peak velocity, mean gradient, and valve area are the standard parameters for severity grading.
Option A is incorrect: all three values fall below the severe threshold — velocity 3.4 m/s, gradient 31 mmHg, and area 1.4 cm² each place this in the moderate category.
Option B is incorrect: velocity 3.8 m/s and gradient 37 mmHg are below the respective severe thresholds (>4 m/s and >40 mmHg), and area 1.2 cm² exceeds the <1.0 cm² threshold.
Option D is incorrect: velocity 4.2 m/s and gradient 42 mmHg exceed their thresholds, but the valve area of 1.1 cm² does not meet the <1.0 cm² criterion, making this set internally discordant and not meeting all three criteria simultaneously.
Slide 23 · Transcript 0:21:22

questions.text: A 77-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis endorses exertional dyspnea and two episodes of near-syncope in the past month. His cardiologist declines a referral for treadmill exercise testing. Separately, the patient asks how long people typically survive without intervention once symptoms like his develop. Which pair of statements is correct?
options: Treadmill exercise testing is safe in symptomatic severe AS because monitoring allows prompt termination; untreated symptomatic AS is a slowly progressive disease with average survival exceeding 10 years
Exercise stress testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS; once symptoms develop, average survival without intervention is only a few years
Exercise testing is recommended in symptomatic AS to objectively assess functional capacity and guide the timing of valve replacement; average survival after symptom onset is 5–10 years
Exercise testing is contraindicated in all aortic stenosis regardless of symptom status; untreated symptomatic AS has a 10-year survival exceeding 60% and rarely requires urgent intervention
questions.explanation:
Exercise stress testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis because it exposes the patient to hemodynamic collapse when a fixed obstruction prevents the cardiac output from meeting exercise demands. The lecture explicitly states: "if you know that valve is severe and patients have symptoms, you don't put them on the treadmill." For natural history, the lecture teaches a long asymptomatic latency period followed by rapid decline: "survival is very short, generally on the order of a few years" once symptoms appear.
Option A is incorrect: monitoring does not make exercise testing safe in symptomatic severe AS; the lecture prohibits it. The "slowly progressive" survival claim contradicts the rapid post-symptom decline the lecture teaches.
Option C is incorrect: the lecture does not recommend exercise testing in symptomatic AS; it explicitly contraindicates it. The 5–10 year survival estimate also substantially overstates the post-symptom prognosis.
Option D is incorrect: exercise testing in carefully selected asymptomatic severe AS patients can be appropriate; blanket contraindication regardless of symptom status is too broad. The survival estimate is also inaccurate.
Slide 26 · Slide 27 · Transcript 0:23:48

questions.text: A 71-year-old woman with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis declines valve replacement and asks about long-term medical management. Her current medications include a statin, a diuretic, and an ACE inhibitor. Which statement most accurately characterizes the role of medical therapy in severe aortic stenosis?
options: Medical therapy does not alter the progression of aortic stenosis and is inferior to valve replacement in severe symptomatic disease
Renin-angiotensin blockade reduces the rate of aortic valve calcification and substantially slows AS progression in randomized controlled trials
Statin therapy reduces inflammatory calcification of the aortic valve and is the recommended disease-modifying treatment for symptomatic AS
Guideline-directed medical therapy achieves outcomes equivalent to valve replacement in patients with mild-to-moderate symptoms of severe AS
questions.explanation:
Medical therapy does not affect the progression of aortic stenosis and is inferior to valve replacement in severe symptomatic disease. The lecture calls this "the important thing to know" about medical therapy in AS. Diuretics, rate control, and rhythm management address symptoms, but no pharmacologic agent has demonstrated disease-modifying effect on AS progression — and none can substitute for valve replacement once symptoms develop.
Option B is incorrect: the lecture states that no pharmacologic therapy has demonstrated disease-modifying effect on AS progression.
Option C is incorrect: statins are used in AS patients according to standard cardiovascular risk guidelines, not as an AS-specific disease-modifying therapy; the lecture explicitly states this distinction.
Option D is incorrect: the lecture explicitly states medical therapy is "inferior to valve replacement" in severe symptomatic AS — there is no demonstrated equivalence.
Slide 29 · Transcript 0:24:48

questions.text: A 62-year-old woman with severe aortic stenosis is entirely asymptomatic and has been monitored with serial echocardiography for 3 years. Her latest echo shows LVEF of 44%. She is also found to have significant coronary artery disease requiring CABG. Which scenario, by itself, constitutes an indication for aortic valve replacement in this asymptomatic patient?
options: She describes mild fatigue with vigorous exertion, which she attributes to normal aging and has not reported as a cardiac symptom to her physician
Serial echocardiography documents a peak transaortic velocity of 4.5 m/s with no change in LVEF and no planned cardiac surgery
She has a valve area of 0.72 cm² on repeat echo with preserved LVEF of 60% and no other cardiac surgery planned
Her LVEF has declined below 50%, or she is scheduled for concurrent cardiac surgery such as CABG that provides an opportunity to replace the valve
questions.explanation:
Asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis has two main indications for valve replacement: LVEF falling below 50%, and the patient undergoing CABG or other cardiac surgery where the valve can be addressed simultaneously. The lecture lists: "Severe AS and LVEF <50%" and "Severe, asymptomatic, and getting CABG (or other heart surgery)." Both apply here — LVEF 44% meets the <50% criterion, and the required CABG provides a second independent indication.
Option A is incorrect: exertional fatigue not reported as a symptom to the physician does not yet meet the AVR threshold in this framing; objective symptom documentation or exercise testing to unmask symptoms would be needed.
Option B is incorrect: a high peak velocity confirms anatomic severity but does not independently indicate AVR in an asymptomatic patient with preserved LVEF and no other qualifying criteria — severity criteria already established the diagnosis.
Option C is incorrect: valve area of 0.72 cm² confirms severe AS but does not by itself trigger AVR in an asymptomatic patient with preserved LVEF and no concomitant surgery planned.
Slide 31 · Transcript 0:26:14

questions.text: A 54-year-old man with bicuspid aortic stenosis undergoes heart valve team evaluation for valve replacement. He asks directly which approach lasts longer — transcatheter (TAVR) or surgical (SAVR). Which statement is correct?
options: TAVR now offers durability equivalent to surgical valves at all ages and is preferred in patients under 65 to minimize reoperation risk
TAVR is less durable than surgical aortic valve replacement, which is a key consideration when selecting the approach in younger patients
Surgical bioprosthetic valves and TAVR devices have identical 15-year durability, making surgical risk the only differentiating factor in valve selection
TAVR valves outlast surgical valves because the catheter-based delivery technique subjects the leaflets to less mechanical trauma during implantation
questions.explanation:
TAVR is less durable than surgical aortic valve replacement, and this trade-off is explicitly taught as a limitation of the transcatheter approach. The lecture states: "overall, not as durable as surgical valves." The professor illustrates this clinically — a younger patient such as a 45-year-old would benefit from a more durable surgical valve, while an older patient may prefer TAVR to avoid surgical morbidity. TAVR indications have expanded to lower-risk populations, but the durability gap remains a meaningful factor in younger patients.
Option A is incorrect: the lecture explicitly states TAVR is "not as durable as surgical valves"; equivalent durability at all ages is not supported by current data or the lecture's teaching.
Option C is incorrect: 15-year TAVR durability data are limited compared with surgical bioprosthetics; the lecture does not support durability equivalence, and the valve selection decision involves more than just surgical risk.
Option D is incorrect: the lecture states the opposite — TAVR is less durable; the proposed biological mechanism is not part of this lecture's teaching and is factually unsupported by available evidence.
Slide 32 · Transcript 0:27:41

questions.text: A 48-year-old man with Marfan syndrome develops moderate-to-severe aortic regurgitation from progressive aortic root dilation. Echocardiography shows LV enlargement with increased wall thickness. Which statement best describes the combined hemodynamic derangement and structural cardiac adaptation in chronic aortic regurgitation?
options: Reduced LV filling volume and concentric wall thickening occur as the ventricle compensates for pressure overload without a significant change in preload

The regurgitant volume raises LV systolic pressure without significantly increasing end-diastolic volume, producing a pattern of concentric hypertrophy similar to that seen in aortic stenosis or other chronic pressure-overload conditions affecting the left heart

The regurgitant volume increases LV end-diastolic volume (raising preload), LV dilation increases wall tension (raising afterload), and the heart compensates with eccentric hypertrophy via sarcomere replication in series
Regurgitant flow directly elevates right atrial pressure via septal shift, triggering reflex fluid retention and biventricular eccentric hypertrophy
questions.explanation:
Chronic aortic regurgitation creates a dual hemodynamic burden: the regurgitant volume increases LV end-diastolic volume (elevated preload), and the resulting LV dilation increases wall tension via the Laplace relationship (elevated afterload). The compensatory structural response is eccentric hypertrophy — "replication of sarcomeres in series and elongation of myocytes to offset increased wall tension," as the lecture states. This contrasts with the concentric hypertrophy of aortic stenosis (sarcomeres in parallel from pressure overload). The forward stroke volume is maintained initially by this compensatory enlargement and increased total stroke volume.
Option A is incorrect: chronic AR characteristically increases, not decreases, LV end-diastolic volume; concentric hypertrophy is the hallmark of AS, not volume overload states.
Option B is incorrect: aortic regurgitation is a volume overload condition; the regurgitant bolus increases end-diastolic volume (preload) rather than driving concentric hypertrophy from pressure overload.
Option D is incorrect: the primary hemodynamic consequence of AR falls on the left ventricle; right atrial pressure elevation and biventricular eccentric hypertrophy are not the primary AR teaching.
Slide 38 · Transcript 0:32:39

questions.text: A 33-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe dyspnea of 12-hour onset. He was treated for infective endocarditis 72 hours ago. Bedside echo shows a non-dilated LV, LVEF of 58%, and markedly elevated LV diastolic pressure on Doppler with early mitral valve closure. You suspect acute aortic regurgitation. Which mechanism best explains this hemodynamic picture?
options: The LV has not had time to adapt to the sudden volume overload, and the abrupt rise in LV diastolic pressure reflects failure of acute compensation
Chronic eccentric remodeling has produced a high-compliance LV that buffers the increased diastolic volume without significant pressure elevation
The regurgitant jet directly elevates right atrial pressure via ventricular septal shift, producing backward failure without significant LV pressure change
Infective endocarditis selectively impairs LV systolic contractility, reducing ejection fraction before any change in LV diastolic pressure occurs
questions.explanation:
In acute aortic regurgitation, the LV does not have time to adapt to the sudden changes in preload and afterload that accompany abrupt, large-volume regurgitation. The lecture states: "LV does not have time to adapt...changes of increased wall thickness, increased cavity size...are things that occur over time." With no chronic adaptation, the non-dilated, non-compliant LV is overwhelmed by the regurgitant volume, producing a marked acute rise in LV diastolic pressure. The normal LV size on echo confirms that chronic eccentric remodeling has not occurred.
Option B is incorrect: high LV compliance with buffered diastolic pressure describes the compensated chronic AR state — the opposite of the acute presentation, where the non-dilated LV behaves as a non-compliant chamber.
Option C is incorrect: septal shift and right atrial pressure elevation are not the primary mechanism of acute AR; the hemodynamic insult is directly the acute rise in LV diastolic pressure from the regurgitant volume.
Option D is incorrect: acute AR causes volume overload of the LV rather than primarily impairing systolic contractility; the preserved LVEF in this case is consistent with acute volume overload rather than systolic dysfunction.
Slide 42 · Transcript 0:35:39

questions.text: A 41-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department acutely ill with dyspnea that began 8 hours ago. Heart rate is 122/min, BP 84/58 mmHg. Her extremities are cold and cyanotic. Chest X-ray shows pulmonary edema without cardiomegaly. Auscultation reveals an early diastolic murmur. You suspect acute aortic regurgitation. Which physical exam profile most accurately reflects this presentation?
options: Wide pulse pressure of 65 mmHg and bounding peripheral pulses, identical to the exam findings expected in chronic AR
Ill-appearing and tachycardic with peripheral vasoconstriction, absent wide pulse pressure, and no cardiomegaly on imaging
Displaced PMI from rapid LV dilation reflecting eccentric hypertrophy, with a loud Austin Flint mid-diastolic rumble at the apex
S3 gallop and systolic murmur from a hyperdynamic LV, combined with bilateral lower extremity edema from chronic right-sided heart failure
questions.explanation:
Acute aortic regurgitation presents with an ill-appearing, tachycardic patient in hemodynamic distress — with peripheral vasoconstriction, cyanosis, pulmonary edema, and notably absent wide pulse pressure — and without the cardiomegaly or displaced PMI seen in chronic AR. The lecture emphasizes: "The most important physical exam feature you'll pick up is just how patients look. So these patients look unwell." Peripheral vasoconstriction narrows the pulse pressure, so the wide pulse pressure of chronic AR is absent. No cardiomegaly reflects that the LV has had no time to dilate, consistent with the normal LV size seen on echo in acute AR.
Option A is incorrect: wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses are hallmarks of chronic AR; in acute AR, intense sympathetic vasoconstriction narrows the pulse pressure.
Option C is incorrect: displaced PMI and Austin Flint murmur reflect a chronically dilated, remodeled LV; neither develops in the acute setting where remodeling has not had time to occur.
Option D is incorrect: S3 gallop with bilateral leg edema describes chronic decompensated disease; the acuity of onset over hours (not weeks) makes chronic right-sided failure an incompatible framing.
Slide 45 · Slide 48 · Transcript 0:38:49

questions.text: A 52-year-old man with chronic aortic regurgitation from rheumatic disease is seen in clinic. BP is 158/50 mmHg, HR 78/min. The point of maximal impulse is displaced to the anterior axillary line in the 6th intercostal space. On auscultation, a high-pitched diastolic murmur begins immediately after S2 and extends through three-quarters of diastole. Which interpretation of these findings is correct?
options: The duration of the diastolic murmur is unrelated to AR severity — it reflects the size of the leaflet defect alone and does not correlate with the hemodynamic gradient
A blood pressure of 158/50 mmHg indicates aortic stenosis as the primary lesion; the diastolic murmur reflects coexisting tricuspid regurgitation from elevated right-sided pressures
The length of the diastolic murmur indicates acute AR, since acute lesions produce longer and higher-pitched murmurs than the equivalent chronic lesions
The wide pulse pressure and laterally displaced PMI reflect LV dilation from volume overload, and a longer diastolic murmur duration indicates more severe chronic AR
questions.explanation:
In chronic aortic regurgitation, wide pulse pressure and a laterally displaced PMI reflect LV volume overload and eccentric dilation, and the duration of the diastolic murmur correlates with severity. The lecture states: "the duration of that murmur is gonna be indicative of more severe aortic regurgitation in the chronic patient." A murmur extending through most of diastole signals that a significant aortic-to-LV pressure gradient persists throughout diastole — a feature of more severe regurgitation. The pulse pressure of 108 mmHg (158 − 50) reflects the large stroke volume and rapid arterial run-off of significant AR.
Option A is incorrect: murmur duration in chronic AR is explicitly taught as a severity marker; it is not unrelated to the degree of regurgitation.
Option B is incorrect: a BP of 158/50 mmHg with wide pulse pressure and an early diastolic murmur immediately after A2 is the classic presentation of AR, not AS; AS would produce a systolic murmur with a narrow pulse pressure.
Option C is incorrect: the lecture specifically teaches that in acute AR the murmur is shorter and lower-pitched; a longer murmur points toward chronic, not acute, AR — option C inverts this relationship.
Slide 46 · Transcript 0:39:04

questions.text: A 46-year-old man with known severe chronic aortic regurgitation attends a follow-up visit. During examination, you observe rhythmic head-nodding synchronous with each heartbeat, and palpation of the femoral artery reveals an abrupt pistol-shot quality pulse. Which named signs, respectively, do these findings represent?
options: Mueller's sign (uvula pulsation) and Duroziez's sign
Quincke's pulses and Hill's sign
de Musset's sign and Corrigan's pulses
Becker's sign and Quincke's pulses
questions.explanation:
The rhythmic head bob synchronous with the heartbeat is de Musset's sign; the abrupt pistol-shot femoral pulse is Corrigan's pulse. The lecture identifies de Musset's sign as "head bob with each systolic pulsation" and Corrigan's pulses as '"pistol shot" pulses over the femoral artery.' Both findings reflect the wide pulse pressure and hyperdynamic circulation of severe chronic AR, where a large stroke volume enters a system with a low diastolic resistance, producing exaggerated pressure oscillations transmitted peripherally.
Option A is incorrect: Mueller's sign is pulsation of the uvula, and Duroziez's sign is a systolic and diastolic bruit over the femoral artery on compression — neither matches rhythmic head-bobbing or a pistol-shot pulse.
Option B is incorrect: Quincke's pulses are capillary pulsations visible in the nailbeds, and Hill's sign is a popliteal BP exceeding brachial BP by more than 60 mmHg — neither matches the described findings.
Option D is incorrect: Becker's sign is pulsation of the retinal arteries and pupils, and Quincke's pulses are nailbed capillary pulsations — neither matches head-bobbing or a pistol-shot femoral pulse.
Slide 47 · Transcript 0:41:01

questions.text: A 36-year-old man undergoes emergent echocardiography for suspected acute aortic regurgitation following a Type A aortic dissection. His LV end-diastolic diameter measures 4.8 cm (normal for size) and LVEF is 62%. Which echocardiographic finding pattern is most characteristic of acute, rather than chronic, aortic regurgitation?
options: Markedly dilated LV with severely reduced LVEF and holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending thoracic aorta, reflecting years of progressive chronic eccentric remodeling from sustained volume overload
Severe eccentric LVH with a wide regurgitant color-Doppler jet and normal aortic-to-LV pressure equalization time on continuous-wave Doppler
LV size and LVEF are normal because the LV has not had time to remodel; Doppler shows a dense regurgitant signal with rapid pressure equalization, and diastolic mitral regurgitation may be present
Hyperdynamic LV with LVEF above 70% and a normal diastolic filling pattern on pulsed-wave Doppler throughout the cardiac cycle
questions.explanation:
In acute aortic regurgitation, the LV has not had time to remodel, so LV size and LVEF are usually normal. The lecture states: "in acute aortic regurgitation, the LV size and ejection fraction are usually gonna be normal. Again, the heart hasn't had a chance to remodel." The Doppler signals are characteristically dense (high regurgitant volume) with rapid pressure equalization between aorta and LV in diastole, as the non-compliant LV diastolic pressure rises quickly to meet the aortic pressure. Diastolic mitral regurgitation — LV diastolic pressure rising above left atrial pressure — may also be present.
Option A is incorrect: a dilated LV with reduced LVEF describes chronic, decompensated AR after years of eccentric remodeling, not the acute presentation where no adaptation has occurred.
Option B is incorrect: severe eccentric LVH reflects chronic volume overload; no significant hypertrophy is present in acute AR; and rapid (not normal) pressure equalization is the characteristic acute Doppler finding.
Option D is incorrect: LVEF above 70% would suggest a hyperdynamic low-afterload state; acute AR increases both preload and afterload, and LVEF is typically normal — not supranormal — because no chronic compensatory changes have developed.
Slide 50 · Transcript 0:43:47

questions.text: A 38-year-old woman is found to have mild-to-moderate aortic regurgitation on echocardiography performed for a murmur. She is asymptomatic with normal LV size and preserved function. A colleague asks about the recommended echocardiographic surveillance schedule — both for this patient now and if she were reclassified as severe AR in the future. Which schedule is correct?
options: Every 5 years for mild-to-moderate AR; every 2 years for severe AR
Every 3 years for mild-to-moderate AR; annually for severe AR
Every 6 months for mild-to-moderate AR; every 3 months for severe AR
Every 1–2 years (mild-to-moderate AR); every 6 months (severe AR)
questions.explanation:
Asymptomatic chronic aortic regurgitation is surveilled with echocardiography every 1–2 years for mild-to-moderate disease and every 6 months for severe disease. The lecture explicitly states both intervals: "if the valve regurgitation is mild to moderate, we're imaging every 1 or 2. If it's severe, you're following it more like every 6 months." The rationale is that severe AR can cause progressive, clinically silent LV dysfunction; closer monitoring captures the window for intervention before irreversible LV damage.
Option A is incorrect: a 5-year interval for mild-to-moderate AR and a 2-year interval for severe AR are both longer than recommended and risk missing clinically important LV changes.
Option B is incorrect: 3 years for mild-to-moderate AR overshoots the guideline; annual imaging for severe AR is less frequent than the recommended 6-month schedule for that severity tier.
Option C is incorrect: 6-month imaging for mild-to-moderate AR is more frequent than needed and imposes unnecessary burden; 3-month intervals for severe AR are not part of the taught protocol.

questions.text: A 53-year-old man with severe chronic aortic regurgitation has been followed with serial echocardiography. He remains entirely asymptomatic. His latest echo shows an LV end-systolic diameter of 53 mm and LVEF of 56%. His cardiologist recommends valve replacement. Which finding in this asymptomatic patient provides the most direct indication for surgery?
options: He is asymptomatic with LVEF preserved above 50%; surgery should be deferred until symptoms develop regardless of chamber dimensions
An LVEF of 56% exceeds the threshold for AVR in asymptomatic AR; valve replacement should be deferred until EF falls below 35%
LV end-systolic diameter of 53 mm exceeds the 50 mm severe LV dilation threshold, which is a surgical indication even in asymptomatic patients
Valve replacement in asymptomatic chronic AR is indicated only after formal treadmill testing has confirmed at least moderate exertional symptoms on objective assessment
questions.explanation:
Severe LV dilation, defined as an LV end-systolic diameter greater than 50 mm, is a surgical indication for AVR in chronic aortic regurgitation even in asymptomatic patients. The lecture lists the AR surgical criteria as: severe regurgitation plus symptoms, LVEF <50%, severe LV dilation (end-systolic >50 mm), or going for another cardiac surgery. This patient's LVESD of 53 mm satisfies the dilation criterion independently, even though LVEF of 56% does not yet trigger the <50% threshold.
Option A is incorrect: preserved LVEF does not preclude AVR when the LVESD criterion is met; waiting for symptoms risks irreversible LV damage, which is why objective size criteria exist.
Option B is incorrect: the LVEF threshold for AVR in chronic AR is <50%, not <35%; an EF of 56% does not trigger surgery on this criterion alone, but the LVESD criterion is independently met.
Option D is incorrect: formal exercise testing is not required for AVR referral in asymptomatic severe AR when objective structural criteria (LVESD, LVEF) are satisfied; the lecture does not impose this requirement.

questions.text: A 29-year-old man with Marfan syndrome presents in hemodynamic shock with acute severe aortic regurgitation from Type A aortic dissection. HR is 126/min, BP 76/52 mmHg. The cardiothoracic surgery team is mobilizing for emergent surgery. Which medical strategy is correct for temporizing this patient while awaiting the operating room?
options: Vasodilator (to reduce SVR and limit regurgitant volume) combined with an inotrope to maintain forward output — surgical intervention is the definitive treatment
IV beta-blocker to reduce heart rate, lower myocardial oxygen demand, and limit the time available for diastolic regurgitation with each beat
Intra-aortic balloon pump placement to augment diastolic coronary perfusion pressure and reduce LV afterload while awaiting the operating room
IV furosemide to relieve pulmonary congestion and supplemental oxygen while monitoring closely for spontaneous hemodynamic stabilization and gradual improvement over several hours of observation
questions.explanation:
Acute aortic regurgitation requires prompt surgical intervention; the bridge to surgery uses a vasodilator (to reduce SVR and limit regurgitant volume per beat) and an inotrope (to support forward cardiac output), while the heart rate is maintained and not slowed. The lecture states: "temporize with vasodilator and inotrope" and explicitly warns: "do not slow the heart rate — prolongs diastole." Tachycardia is compensatory in acute AR because it shortens diastole and limits regurgitation time. The intra-aortic balloon pump and Impella are contraindicated because they raise aortic diastolic pressure, worsening regurgitation.
Option B is incorrect: beta-blockers slow heart rate, prolonging diastole and worsening the regurgitant volume per beat; the lecture explicitly prohibits heart rate reduction in acute AR management.
Option C is incorrect: the intra-aortic balloon pump is explicitly contraindicated in acute AR — it inflates in diastole, raising aortic pressure and worsening the regurgitation; the same applies to Impella devices.
Option D is incorrect: while diuresis can relieve congestion symptomatically, it does not address the hemodynamic emergency and does not constitute appropriate bridge therapy; spontaneous improvement should not be awaited in a condition with high mortality without surgery.
